blocks.text: Here are the Vim forks I know about:
Neovim: “a Vim-based text editor engineered for extensibility and usability, to encourage new applications and contributions.”
Vim Classic: “a stable, long-term support fork of the ubiquitous text editor, maintained without the assistance of generative AI tools.”
EVi: “a hard-fork of Vim v9.1.0 (Jan 2024) before AI was used in the project.”
MacVim: “a macOS version of the Vim text editor, providing a graphical user interface for Vim, while tightly integrating with macOS and providing features specific to the platform.”
This list doesn’t include Vim-inspired editors like Kakoune, Vim-style plugins for other editors like IdeaVim, or Vim “distributions” like LazyVim.
Contact me if you know of other forks!

blocks.text: Chan Karunamuni

iPhone Duo is here! Excited to have worked on the design of our open/close transition. It’s designed to make the two displays feel like one seamless experience by perceptually bending the focal plane, not the content, so that it feels like opening a window onto a singular view.

topPicks.title: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology
topPicks.titleZh: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology
topPicks.summary: Elon Musk Just Gave Europe a Reason to Replace American Technology

blocks.text: I’ve been in London for the last month and have heard policymakers react to the wake up call Elon Musk just delivered.

The decision of the U.S. to shut off intelligence and throttle the military version of Starlink called Starshield to Ukraine may have been a blip in the news in the US, but it has sent tremors across Europe.

For years doomsayers in the UK and Europe were worried about the U.S. having a kill switch in weapon systems and critical commercial technology that could disconnect them at will. Most people, including me, thought that it was a paranoid fantasy.

Until it happened. Seemingly on a whim of a single individual, (according to the Wall Street Journal) Elon Musk personally ordered the restrictions, and the effect was to tilt Russia’s war against Ukraine in favor of the Russians. This wasn’t an articulated U.S. foreign policy nor was it an announced act of the U.S. government. From news accounts it appears to have been a personal decision of an American CEO acting unilaterally.

Blowback
For whatever reason, whether it was to satisfy a request from the White House or some personal animosity to the Ukrainians, from Europe’s perspective, that’s almost beside the point. An American company operating critical military infrastructure was able to degrade the capability of an American partner in the middle of a war. Without warning.
The message heard loud and clear here in Europe was that the U.S. is an unreliable security and technology partner willing to throw any partner under the bus, at any time, for any reason.

The conversations I’ve heard have included, “what happens if other U.S. CEOs – Microsoft, OpenAI or Anthropic, Oracle, Palantir, or Google – decide to restrict/limit or deny access to their products? What capabilities would Europe lose if enterprise software and/or AI across Europe goes dark?” This was a laughable scenario until this week. To a lot of European decision makers, it is no longer outside the realm of possibility.
The lesson that was brought home was that no nation, Europe or elsewhere, can continue to outsource its national sovereignty and security by depending solely on US data systems or intelligence.

Unintended Consequences
Besides the political ramifications, the business ones are going to come home to roost. If every U.S. vendor is now a kill-switch risk, the allied market for that whole ecosystem shrinks. As it sinks into the European countries that the U.S, can simply shut off any technology, over time they will find and build alternatives. In the years ahead, this may cost American companies tens if not hundreds of billions of lost revenue.

Europe has been debating digital sovereignty for years. Up to this year, the idea of cloning the capabilities of the best U.S. products seemed like an insurmountable problem. And some, like low-cost access to space, still are. But today AI collapses the cost of creating sovereign software at exactly the time that geopolitical risk is increasing customers’ willingness to switch. AI makes recreating the features, functions and compatibility of Microsoft Office, Oracle, Salesforce, Palantir, Anduril, et al. within reach. AI puts it well within the capabilities of most nations.

The U.S. spent decades establishing itself as the world’s indispensable technology supplier. A substantial part of that advantage depended on customers believing American technology would remain reliable and available.

Going forward a U.S. founder selling into European defense or government now needs an answer to “who holds the switch” before the first meeting; and European founders just got sovereignty as a sellable feature.
What was done in a fit of pique will cost the U.S. both leadership and jobs.
Filed under: National Security, Teaching |

blocks.text: Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure and industrial technology. This week we look at minimum lot sizes, Boeing’s next 737 MAX, Fervo short sellers, Figure AI’s training data, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.
No essay this week, but I’m working on a piece about manufacturing isotopes that should be out next week.
Almost two thirds of US homebuilders said immigration enforcement is affecting their labor force, up from 23% in March and 13% a year ago. [WSJ]

I had always heard of “minimum lot sizes” as one of the many land-use regulations that restricts the supply of new housing, but I had no idea how extensive they were. But a new report from AEI claims that 90% of jurisdictions have some sort of minimum lot size, and that this is a major barrier to constructing smaller, less expensive starter homes. [AEI]
Canadian real house prices have more than doubled since 2005. [CMHC]
Airbnb bans making guests do the dishes and take out the trash. [The Verge]

The Wall Street Journal on rising pedestrian deaths on US roads. It places the blame chiefly on road design, though it doesn’t explain why road design would cause a sudden uptick around 2009. [WSJ] See also my previous essays about US pedestrian deaths.

The market share of modular and panelized housing construction in the US remains very low. “The total market share of non-site-built single-family homes (modular and panelized) was just 3% of single-family homes in 2025, according to NAHB analysis of completion data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Survey of Construction (SOC). This matched the 3% market share recorded in both 2023 and 2024.” [NAHB]
The FAA certifies another version of Boeing’s 737 MAX, the 737-10. Boeing currently has 1555 orders for it. [Boeing]

Worries about the shipbuilding gap between the US and China often focus on commercial ship output (of which the US has virtually none), but it seems that there’s also a substantial gap in naval vessel output. “The combined tonnage of combat ships built by China in the two years through to December 2025 amounted to 636,208 tons, compared to 270,509 tons for the United States, according to data compiled by Flottes de Combat and French maritime industry association Gican.” [Defense News]
Former Tesla executive Drew Baglino’s solid-state transformer startup, Heron Power, signs an agreement for 1 GW worth of manufacturing capacity for data center developer Vantage. [Heron Power]

Is optical fiber going to be the next data center-induced shortage? “Tightening supply is projected to push spot prices for finished optical fiber products to 2.8–5 times their 2025 levels or higher. In response, telecom operators are shifting from short-term purchasing to long-term supply agreements (LTAs) to lock in fiber supply early.” [TrendForce]
Helium has been re-added to the US’s list of critical materials. A good time to revisit my piece on why helium is hard to replace. [X]

Seems bad. “[T]he U.S. aluminum industry, the world’s leading supplier just 25 years ago, produces a mere 1% of global output today. Moreover, there are zero operating smelters in the United States—or in a NATO country—capable of producing the high-purity aluminum required for military applications; the only comparable sources—China, Russia, and the United Arab Emirates—are highly precarious.“ [American Primary Aluminum Association]

Former OpenAI research chief Bob McGrew’s manufacturing startup Arda, which is doing manufacturing automation, raises $160 million. ““When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design,” McGrew said. “We’ve built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster.”” [CNBC]

topPicks.title: Book Review: Get Ahead of Being Dead by Evie King ★★★★☆
topPicks.titleZh: Book Review: Get Ahead of Being Dead by Evie King ★★★★☆
topPicks.summary: Book Review: Get Ahead of Being Dead by Evie King ★★★★☆

blocks.text: After reading Evie King's previous book Ashes To Admin - Tales from the Caseload of a Council Funeral Officer I was eager to read her not-quite-a-sequel.

We know what happens after death; paperwork. Gas bills need to be cancelled, funeral wishes need to be carried out, money needs to be apportioned between warring family members. When you die, you won't be there to experience the annoyance and distress - but other people will. So do you help them or not?
This book is a chatty and informal guide to how to set out your wishes - including that you have no wishes.
Much like her previous book, it cheerfully mixes anecdotes about death with a powerful political message about how we treat the dead (and, I suppose, nearly dead).

It is one of those rare eBooks which is probably better as a paper book because the end of every chapter has a few dozen questions to fill in. Some are seemingly banal (library card number) and other potentially a little distressing (who do you not want invited to your funeral). The aim is to keep the answers somewhere prominent so that, come the inevitable, there's a one-stop-shop for all your deadmin.

Evie does an excellent job of making the slightly terrifying first steps accessible and approachable. It's fully trans, non-binary, and poly inclusive. It doesn't shy away from some of the more uncomfortable aspects of death, but it really does feel like the author is having a coffee & natter with you.

The style won't be for everyone. I think I'd rather have this as just a plain list of questions. But, then again, I did find it compelling to read the stories about what happens when things go wrong. So maybe I don't know myself as well as I think. Say, what song do I want playing at my funeral?
There's no doubt this is a slightly challenging and provocative read - but you should absolutely buy a copy for yourself and fill it in. Whether you buy it for your friends and relatives…

blocks.text: In 1982, computers seemed like a thing in the future for the majority of people. But Commodore was doing what they could to make them affordable. After creating the first color computer that would sell for less than $300, the first 64k computer to sell for less than $600, and the first disk drive for less than $300, Commodore wanted a sub-$100 modem to go with all of that. They outsourced the design to Anchor Automation, and the VICmodem, model 1600, was what they came up with. It reached the market in March 1982.
The first modem that cost less than $100

The information age was very much in its infancy, but if you didn’t want to miss it, a VIC-20 with a cassette drive and a VICmodem would let you participate at the lowest possible price. Ex-Commodore executive Michael Tomczyk claims it was the first modem to sell a million units, but I’ve never seen one with higher than a six-digit serial number, so that figure may be a little optimistic. I think they sold closer to 140,000 of them.

The 1600 VICmodem was about as basic of a modem as you could get. The main component on its PCB was a Motorola MC14412, and there were only six other chips on the board. Commodore being Commodore, they cut the price aggressively.
Limitations of the Commodore 1600 VICmodem

The VICmodem’s biggest limitation was its inability to dial the phone on its own. Acoustic coupler modems weren’t uncommon at the time. With an acoustic modem, you dialed the phone, then placed the handset on cups so the modem could, essentially, talk and listen on the phone using a speaker and a microphone. It was cheaper than building an autodial-type modem.

But Commodore couldn’t meet the price point it wanted with an acoustic coupler modem. Instead, after you picked up the phone, dialed it, and heard a modem carrier, you unplugged the handset and plugged the cord into the back of the 1600. This let them eliminate the speaker and microphone, reducing the parts count.

In theory this could give a cleaner signal than you would get from an acoustic coupler. In practice, I don’t know how much difference it made. My 1600 was very noisy, much noiser than the 1670 I replaced it with.

And by noisy, I mean garbled characters on the screen. If you got a clean signal, the text was very readable. But if the signal wasn’t clean, you got random characters mixed in with whatever your transmitting. That was why you needed a protocol like Ward Christensen‘s Xmodem to transfer files.

This wasn’t the way most other modems on the market operated, but since Commodore came into a small market and flooded it with an estimated 140,000 units, that gave them some sway in defining how a modem was expected to operate, at least until it became possible to build more capable modems and hit that $100 price point.
And that ended up being a problem, especially in Canada.
The phone problem

The other problem with this approach was not all phones had modular handsets. Rotary phones with hardwired handsets were still very common in 1982-86, so the 1600 wasn’t much of a bargain if your phone didn’t work with it. Commodore had an adapter to solve that, called the VIC-1605, which has a story of its own.

In Canada, Commodore bundled the 1600 with a special phone with a Commodore logo on the front, Northern Telecom’s version of the Western Electric 500. Problem was, it was a rotary phone with a hardwired handset, so you couldn’t use it with the 1600, defeating the purpose. Commodore didn’t realize this until they’d already taken delivery.
That was a problem. But it turned out Commodore had another problem. A bigger problem. A legal problem.

It turns out that modular handsets were illegal in Canada at the time. To solve the problem Commodore found itself in, Commodore came up with the VIC-1605, an adapter with an RJ-9 jack for the VICmodem and two RJ-11 jacks. This let customers plug the phone directly into the modem, and then plug the modem into the wall. Then they could dial the phone, then flip a switch on the adapter when they heard the carrier, and the modem took over.

As far as I know, Commodore didn’t include the VIC-1605 with the VICmodem unless they bundled it with the phone, which is a shame. I don’t know how many other people did this, but I bought a VICmodem without knowing it wouldn’t work with any of our household phones, which all had hardwired handsets.
The Canadian Commodore logo phone is a prized collectible today.
What the Commodore VICmodem was like

Aside from the RJ-9 jack to plug your phone cord into, the 1600 just had a red LED on the side and a slide switch that you used to tell the modem if you were making or receiving a call. More sophisticated modems took a command and knew from the command you used whether it was originating or answering a call. But the VICmodem had to be told.

Realistically, Commodore’s later 1650 modem was a better value because it included dialing capabilities and didn’t rely on your phone. If you had to buy a different phone to use the 1600, then the 1650 usually ended up being cheaper.

Commodore closed out its remaining stock of 1600 VICmodems in 1986. C.O.M.B. Liquidators sold them for $19 apiece, which seemed like a ridiculously low price for a modem at the time. That was especially true if you didn’t know the catch, that you needed a modular phone. C.O.M.B. was where we got ours. In its advertising and in its catalog, C.O.M.B. clearly showed the modem connected to a phone, but didn’t mention anywhere that it required a modular handset. If you were excited at the possibility of getting a modem at a super low price, it was really easy to overlook that detail. Or at least I overlooked it. That was how I got mine, and while I used commercial services like Compuserve and Q-Link, I ended up mostly using bulletin boards. Including to pirate software.
The 1600’s legacy

The 1600 was a minimum viable product even by 1982 standards, so by 1986 it was really outmoded. But it provided consumers an introduction to telecommunications at the lowest possible price for about 4-5 years. You could buy one, decide if it was something you were going to use regularly, then upgrade to something better like a 1670.

And let’s talk about that Canada thing. I don’t know about anyone else, but I find it amusing that the modem was technically illegal in Canada if you used it the way Commodore and Anchor Automation originally intended. Things were changing faster than the law could keep up with. That was one of the things that made the early 1980s great.

As for Anchor Automation, they went on to produce other modems for Commodore computers, some of which it sold under its own brand name. If you had a Commodore 64, 128, or VIC-20 in the 1980s, it’s possible your first modem was another modem made by Anchor Automation, even if you didn’t have a VICmodem.
Value of a Commodore 1600 VICmodem

I don’t like giving valuation opinions but I’ve studied the VICmodem enough to give one in this case. A loose VICmodem is worth less than $10. An example with a low serial number may be worth a bit more, or it might just sell more quickly.

The most I’ve seen a boxed example sell for is $36. A boxed, complete example with a receipt and all the paperwork is interesting, but condition will be key to getting top dollar. A ratty box is worth more than no box, but the closer the box looks to like-new condition, the more it’s worth.

And if you’re looking to sell one, showing the serial number seems to help. I’m not sure if that’s because people are interested in the serial number, or because it’s a good way to gauge its condition. The serial number seems to be more fragile than the rest of the printing, based on examples I’ve observed.

The VICmodem is rarer than the computers it came with. But there’s not a ton of demand for it either, since there’s not really any use for one these days. It’s super slow and the phone lines it worked with are increasingly uncommon. It’s a curiosity, and the few hundred people who are interested in one, like me, probably already have one.

I’ve been tracking VICmodems on Ebay for years, trying to figure out how many were built. Prices are all over the place. I’ve seen lots of them listed for $50. I’ve never seen one sell for that. And I’ve seen some listen on Ebay for 4 years now, with no takers. That tells me the price is too high.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

That was a problem. But it turned out Commodore had another problem. A bigger problem. A legal problem.

It turns out that modular handsets were illegal in Canada at the time. To solve the problem Commodore found itself in, Commodore came up with the VIC-1605, an adapter with an RJ-9 jack for the VICmodem and two RJ-11 jacks. This let customers plug the phone directly into the modem, and then plug the modem into the wall. Then they could dial the phone, then flip a switch on the adapter when they heard the carrier, and the modem took over.

As far as I know, Commodore didn’t include the VIC-1605 with the VICmodem unless they bundled it with the phone, which is a shame. I don’t know how many other people did this, but I bought a VICmodem without knowing it wouldn’t work with any of our household phones, which all had hardwired handsets.
The Canadian Commodore logo phone is a prized collectible today.
What the Commodore VICmodem was like

Aside from the RJ-9 jack to plug your phone cord into, the 1600 just had a red LED on the side and a slide switch that you used to tell the modem if you were making or receiving a call. More sophisticated modems took a command and knew from the command you used whether it was originating or answering a call. But the VICmodem had to be told.

Realistically, Commodore’s later 1650 modem was a better value because it included dialing capabilities and didn’t rely on your phone. If you had to buy a different phone to use the 1600, then the 1650 usually ended up being cheaper.

Commodore closed out its remaining stock of 1600 VICmodems in 1986. C.O.M.B. Liquidators sold them for $19 apiece, which seemed like a ridiculously low price for a modem at the time. That was especially true if you didn’t know the catch, that you needed a modular phone. C.O.M.B. was where we got ours. In its advertising and in its catalog, C.O.M.B. clearly showed the modem connected to a phone, but didn’t mention anywhere that it required a modular handset. If you were excited at the possibility of getting a modem at a super low price, it was really easy to overlook that detail. Or at least I overlooked it. That was how I got mine, and while I used commercial services like Compuserve and Q-Link, I ended up mostly using bulletin boards. Including to pirate software.
The 1600’s legacy

The 1600 was a minimum viable product even by 1982 standards, so by 1986 it was really outmoded. But it provided consumers an introduction to telecommunications at the lowest possible price for about 4-5 years. You could buy one, decide if it was something you were going to use regularly, then upgrade to something better like a 1670.

And let’s talk about that Canada thing. I don’t know about anyone else, but I find it amusing that the modem was technically illegal in Canada if you used it the way Commodore and Anchor Automation originally intended. Things were changing faster than the law could keep up with. That was one of the things that made the early 1980s great.

As for Anchor Automation, they went on to produce other modems for Commodore computers, some of which it sold under its own brand name. If you had a Commodore 64, 128, or VIC-20 in the 1980s, it’s possible your first modem was another modem made by Anchor Automation, even if you didn’t have a VICmodem.
Value of a Commodore 1600 VICmodem

I don’t like giving valuation opinions but I’ve studied the VICmodem enough to give one in this case. A loose VICmodem is worth less than $10. An example with a low serial number may be worth a bit more, or it might just sell more quickly.

The most I’ve seen a boxed example sell for is $36. A boxed, complete example with a receipt and all the paperwork is interesting, but condition will be key to getting top dollar. A ratty box is worth more than no box, but the closer the box looks to like-new condition, the more it’s worth.

And if you’re looking to sell one, showing the serial number seems to help. I’m not sure if that’s because people are interested in the serial number, or because it’s a good way to gauge its condition. The serial number seems to be more fragile than the rest of the printing, based on examples I’ve observed.

The VICmodem is rarer than the computers it came with. But there’s not a ton of demand for it either, since there’s not really any use for one these days. It’s super slow and the phone lines it worked with are increasingly uncommon. It’s a curiosity, and the few hundred people who are interested in one, like me, probably already have one.

I’ve been tracking VICmodems on Ebay for years, trying to figure out how many were built. Prices are all over the place. I’ve seen lots of them listed for $50. I’ve never seen one sell for that. And I’ve seen some listen on Ebay for 4 years now, with no takers. That tells me the price is too high.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

blocks.text: This week’s package management news, and what a week it’s been, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me.
The compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs led to security releases from dozens of package managers, language runtimes and CA bundles this week.
Security

eMudhra generated eight of its intermediate CA certificates in a way that lets anyone recover their private keys. Browsers blocked them through their revocation lists, and tools that bundle their own copy of the roots shipped new releases. I wrote about where those copies end up, and how many critical packages bundle a CA file, in Trust Stores Are Dependencies Too. The disclosure page keeps a table of patched software with version numbers, including ca-certificates updates for most Linux distributions and the BSDs. The package management releases with the fix:
uv 0.13.4 updates the roots compiled into uv, and 0.13.5 updates the managed CPython builds so their pip and ensurepip carry certifi 2026.10.19
Seth Larson’s notice for Python users lists the minimum versions of certifi, pip, uv, sigstore, conda and pixi, and gives a hash-pinned command for upgrading pip from an affected environment
conda 26.9.4 requires the updated certifi and ca-certificates, and the conda blog has update instructions for conda, Mamba and Pixi
pixi 0.82.1
rustup 1.29.2

Root bundles that other packages vendor: certifi 2026.10.19, webpki-roots and webpki-root-certs 1.0.10, rustls-webpki 0.103.16, Elixir castore 1.0.22, Erlang certifi 2.18.0, Perl Mozilla::CA 20261020, Composer ca-bundle 1.6.0 and 1.4.16 and the curl CA bundle
Homebrew’s ca-certificates formula
Java 27.0.1, 25.0.5, 21.0.13, 17.0.21, 11.0.33 and 8u511 for OpenJDK and Oracle JDK

Node.js 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4 update the bundled root certificates to NSS 3.131.1 and fix ten CVEs, four of them rated high, including a Brotli decoder out-of-bounds write that can lead to remote code execution
Hex 2.5.4 removes three emSign roots from its bundled CA list
Composer 2.11.0-RC1 rejects the intermediates even when the system CA store includes their roots
Deno 2.9.8 and Bun 1.4.4
pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish 1.14.3
pnpm 11.28.8 embeds Node.js 26.12.1 in the standalone @pnpm/exe builds
Verdaccio 6.10.7 for its Docker image
Docker Engine 29.9.2 and Docker Desktop 4.96.2
Git for Windows 2.56.0.3
OpenTofu 1.13.2 and 1.12.9
Terraform 1.16.7

For software already installed, EasyBuild maintainers published a script that scans for and removes the untrusted roots from EasyBuild installations. An option scans every .pem and .crt file under a given path.
Michał Górny listed the places a Python user has to upgrade:
certifi in every virtual environment and lockfile, with certifi excluded from dependency cooldowns
the certifi bundled in pip
the pip wheel that ships with Python for ensurepip
Rust tools such as uv that compile in their own copy of the roots
Gentoo’s certifi package uses the system certificates, its pip package uses that certifi, and its Python uses a system ensurepip wheel. Upgrading those packages updates the system install.

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 (PHP Foundation) fix two remote code execution bugs in memory management and error handling. One can be triggered by an unauthenticated request on Apache with mod_php before any application code runs. The post explains that the root cause of the out-of-memory bug was first spotted during the 2024 Quarkslab audit, and the fix stalled for months while the security team weighed competing approaches. The CVE IDs leaked on 20 October, so the release moved forward a day. Chainguard broke the embargo, publishing images containing the fix more than six hours before the coordinated release. Special thanks to Volker Dusch, who leads the PHP Foundation’s Ecosystem Security Team, for his work behind the scenes on this release.

In the project’s second compromise this year, LiteLLM 1.107.0 (Socket) was published to PyPI and GHCR with .pth and sitecustomize.py startup files that collect cloud credentials, SSH keys and coding agent auth files on every Python startup, including programs that never import LiteLLM. The container image’s build provenance records the source repository as Berri-AI/litellm, one hyphen away from the real BerriAI/litellm, and the payload files are absent from the release tag in the real repository. LiteLLM’s maintainers told Help Net Security that the attacker used what appear to be stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens for three engineers’ accounts. The attacker changed the release pipeline and triggered the release from the first, approved it from the second, and deleted the workflow records from the third.

Bloom Security found that npm’s Trusted Publishing matched configurations on the owner/repo name instead of the permanent numeric IDs GitHub includes in the OIDC token. After a maintainer renamed or deleted the bound repository, anyone could register the freed name and publish new versions of the package, with a valid provenance attestation naming their own repository, an exposure Bloom counted across more than 1,500 packages. GitHub’s fix, announced on 2 October, expires any configuration that goes 48 hours without validation. According to npm’s documentation, the first publish binds a configuration to the repository’s immutable identity.

Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 fix bugs in the Onigmo regular expression engine that GitLab turned into remote code execution through user-supplied patterns, such as those in CI configuration. GitLab had already patched the Ruby it ships and assigned four CVEs. The bugs affect applications that pass attacker-controlled strings to Regexp.new or interpolate them into a regexp literal, and they remain exploitable with Regexp.timeout and pattern length limits in place. The four CVEs are GitLab’s, and the Ruby core team plans to discuss whether compiling untrusted patterns is a supported use case.

GitHub package firewall is in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud. It is a proxy between the upstream registry and CI runners, coding agents or internal registries. It checks metadata requests and downloads against an enterprise policy covering cooldown periods, malware and vulnerability advisories, and attestation downgrades. It supports npm only for now, and is free during the preview.

The curl project will make LOW and MEDIUM severity vulnerability reports public on the GitHub issue tracker from 26 October, keeping embargoes only for HIGH and CRITICAL issues. Daniel Stenberg wrote that the project received 13 vulnerability reports on a single Saturday, more than the small security team can handle in private.
Releases

Hex 2.6 adds Workload Identity, so a GitHub Actions job can publish a package or fetch an organisation’s private packages with its OIDC token instead of a stored key. Package builds are now reproducible, and the build_env metadata field records the Hex version needed to rebuild one and compare checksums. Policy overrides can accept a single advisory, retirement reason or the cooldown, mix hex.audit --policy applies the policy to packages already in mix.lock, and mix hex.audit can write SARIF for GitHub code scanning. Hex has dropped stored keys for organisation repositories. In CI, mix hex.organization auth ORGANIZATION --key KEY exchanges the key for a token that lasts about 25 minutes. Organisation admins can now require two-factor authentication for every member.

Composer 2.11.0-RC1 adds a cooldown policy that withholds newly released versions for a configurable period, and a block-scope option so custom policies can also block during install. It now escapes package-controlled paths and shebangs embedded in bin proxies, and stops sending custom repository headers to dist URLs on other hosts whose names start with the repository host. It also removes the source-fallback option added in 2.10.

pnpm 12.15 adds lockfile.integrityTarget: tar, which pins the hash of each package’s uncompressed tar so the lockfile stays the same when a registry recompresses tarballs. It accepts zstd-compressed registry responses and lets pnpm-workspace.yaml load settings from other files and from config dependencies through an include field. pnpm install now fails with ERR_PNPM_REGISTRY_NAME_MISMATCH when a registry returns metadata for a different package than the one requested. Before, pnpm installed it under the name in the metadata, which bypassed allowBuilds rules for the requested name.

mise 2026.10.13 to 2026.10.18 ignores [settings] from untrusted project configs as of 2026.10.13, so a cloned repository’s mise.toml changes settings like node.mirror_url only after mise trust. 2026.10.15 applies the default 24-hour minimum_release_age to every backend, including asdf, vfox, conda and http: tools, and 2026.10.18 adds mise lsp, a language server for mise.toml.

vlt 1.5 adds vlt skills, which links the agent skills that installed dependencies ship into .agents/skills and .claude/skills. An allow-skills query in vlt.json selects which packages’ skills get linked, and the default :not(:malware) query also excludes packages still waiting for a Socket scan. vlt 1.6 adds --global installs and parses ^0, ^0.x and ^0.0 as ranges instead of the exact version 0.0.0.

Bun 1.4.4 migrates Yarn Berry lockfiles to bun.lock with every pinned version preserved. bun install now retries with exponential backoff, where 1.4.3 ran all five retries within 5 ms, and the release closes 133 bun install issues.

uv 0.13.2 to 0.13.5 removes exponential work when simplifying and exporting complex dependency markers and reduces resolver memory use for large graphs. pylock.toml exports now include supported environment restrictions, and the wheel-variants preview fetches and validates PEP 825 index-level variant metadata.

pixi 0.83 adds support for virtual package detectors, which channels will be able to register for virtual packages beyond pixi’s built-in set. pixi prompts for confirmation before running a detector and lists detectors in pixi info.
Mamba 2.10 removes its TUF implementation and mamba-content-trust and completes the exclude_newer policy. It also fixes authentication tokens being dropped on package downloads since 2.9.0.
Athens 0.20 proxies and caches Go toolchain downloads from go.dev/dl under /dl/, and serves cached @latest results in offline and fallback modes.
Terraform 1.17 supports variables and locals in provider requirements and makes Terraform Policy generally available, with a -policies flag for plan, apply and query.

Dependabot now supports npm 12, pnpm 11 and 12, and Bun 1.4. When pnpm 12 writes pnpm-lock.yaml as two YAML documents, the dependency graph misses those dependencies for now, so Dependabot skips alerts and security updates for them and may close existing alerts. Alert responses in the REST API now include a version_requirement field with the version Dependabot recorded.
Also out:
Homebrew 7.0.10
Gradle 9.8.2
pipx 1.18.4
PSResourceGet 1.3.0-rc1
Harbor 2.14.6
ORAS 1.3.5
Papers

Sign Here: Attributing a Source for a More Trustworthy Software Supply Chain (Derek Garcia et al., arXiv) tests whether building only packages that link to a buildable source repository would keep malware out. Across 47,066 known malicious npm and PyPI packages, checking for a source blocked between 87.7% and 99.9% of them depending on how strictly the source was vetted, while 47.4% of a sample of benign packages pointed to a source a user could build from.

Vibenix: Agentic Software Packaging and Maintenance with Nix (Martim Monis et al., arXiv) is an LLM agent that writes Nix packaging expressions through a build-and-repair loop. It produced buildable packages for 95.3% of 466 tasks with Claude Haiku 4.5, against 5.6% for a single-shot tool, though manual checks found only 47% of a sample worked correctly before a refinement step added 35 percentage points.

What Is Under the Hood? A Cross-Ecosystem Study of Vulnerable Dependencies in Construction Software (Mahzabin Tamanna et al., arXiv) ran OSV-Scanner over 904 construction-industry GitHub repositories. OSV-Scanner could scan 54.6% of them, and 80% of those had at least one dependency with a published advisory. Two upstream package families reached about 70% of the affected repositories.
Elsewhere

Sentry gave $1,000,000 to open source maintainers (Vlad Miricioiu, Sentry) this year, up from $750,000. $495,000 went through thanks.dev and $100,000 through ecosyste.ms Funds, which I run, with the rest to foundations including the PSF, PHP Foundation, Ruby Central and Packagist. The Open Source Pledge’s 37 member companies have now paid $8,421,535 to maintainers and foundations.

Farid Zakaria’s One store, two frontends uses $ORIGIN support in PT_INTERP, which he worked on with Christian Brauner for Linux 7.3, to make nixpkgs outputs relocatable so Bazel and buck2 remote executors can use them without Nix installed. In No quarter for gaps he writes gemlock.nix, a Nix side for Bundler lockfiles with platform-specific gems. The bundix pull request that the nixpkgs manual points to for this was opened in 2019 and closed unmerged in August. Who wrote this byte? adds rewind blame to Rewind VM, his deterministic virtual machine for recording and replaying builds. Given two runs with different outputs, rewind blame reports the process that wrote the first differing byte.
Paul Battley has archived the repositories of all his Ruby gems and linked them to a post explaining why he has stopped working on them.
GitRoot 0.5.0 replaces plugin download URLs with Package URLs, a breaking change for existing forge configurations.
zizmor 1.32.0-rc1 adds experimental support for GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles, and William Woodruff is asking for testers with repositories that already use one.

Josh Bressers talks to CyberScoop’s Safe Mode podcast about running VulnCheck’s coordinated disclosure as AI-generated reports increase. He also covers how much less effort it now takes to find vulnerabilities than to fix them.
git-pkgs
I tagged 10 repos this week:
certs v0.1.0 (new), a Go library and CLI for listing X.509 certificates and trust stores in files and package archives
archives v0.10.0
cooldown v0.3.0
enrichment v0.7.3
magic v0.6.0
markup v0.1.2
proxy v0.10.0
purl v0.1.23
registries v0.11.0
sbom v0.1.7
Send links for next week to @[email protected].

Vibenix: Agentic Software Packaging and Maintenance with Nix (Martim Monis et al., arXiv) is an LLM agent that writes Nix packaging expressions through a build-and-repair loop. It produced buildable packages for 95.3% of 466 tasks with Claude Haiku 4.5, against 5.6% for a single-shot tool, though manual checks found only 47% of a sample worked correctly before a refinement step added 35 percentage points.

What Is Under the Hood? A Cross-Ecosystem Study of Vulnerable Dependencies in Construction Software (Mahzabin Tamanna et al., arXiv) ran OSV-Scanner over 904 construction-industry GitHub repositories. OSV-Scanner could scan 54.6% of them, and 80% of those had at least one dependency with a published advisory. Two upstream package families reached about 70% of the affected repositories.
Elsewhere

Sentry gave $1,000,000 to open source maintainers (Vlad Miricioiu, Sentry) this year, up from $750,000. $495,000 went through thanks.dev and $100,000 through ecosyste.ms Funds, which I run, with the rest to foundations including the PSF, PHP Foundation, Ruby Central and Packagist. The Open Source Pledge’s 37 member companies have now paid $8,421,535 to maintainers and foundations.

Farid Zakaria’s One store, two frontends uses $ORIGIN support in PT_INTERP, which he worked on with Christian Brauner for Linux 7.3, to make nixpkgs outputs relocatable so Bazel and buck2 remote executors can use them without Nix installed. In No quarter for gaps he writes gemlock.nix, a Nix side for Bundler lockfiles with platform-specific gems. The bundix pull request that the nixpkgs manual points to for this was opened in 2019 and closed unmerged in August. Who wrote this byte? adds rewind blame to Rewind VM, his deterministic virtual machine for recording and replaying builds. Given two runs with different outputs, rewind blame reports the process that wrote the first differing byte.
Paul Battley has archived the repositories of all his Ruby gems and linked them to a post explaining why he has stopped working on them.
GitRoot 0.5.0 replaces plugin download URLs with Package URLs, a breaking change for existing forge configurations.
zizmor 1.32.0-rc1 adds experimental support for GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles, and William Woodruff is asking for testers with repositories that already use one.

Josh Bressers talks to CyberScoop’s Safe Mode podcast about running VulnCheck’s coordinated disclosure as AI-generated reports increase. He also covers how much less effort it now takes to find vulnerabilities than to fix them.

blocks.text: I added four player online mode to Battledrones - previous maps were limited to two.
Here's the initial prompt I used:

Add a new map for a four player battle - four way rotational symmetry, up to four AI players, works with the WebSocket non-audio based multiplayer mode so up to four human players can join (any spare slots use AI)
Claude Opus 5.5 added a new map called "Compass Rose" and modified the WebSockets multiplayer network code to support up to four players for that map, joining via share links or QR codes.
The new teams use robots themed in purple and green, joining the existing blue and red designs. You can preview those colors in the updated model browser.
Here's a replay link to watch a four way AI battle with the "Goliath Armada" mutator turned on, where each side starts with four giant Goliath mech units.

topPicks.title: Interesting systemd features you may not know about
topPicks.titleZh: Interesting systemd features you may not know about
topPicks.summary: Interesting systemd features you may not know about

blocks.text: I've always thought of systemd as a fairly boring piece of plumbing, that boots your system and runs background services. I also knew there was enormous controversy when it first came out, but I hadn't really dived much into it past this.
Systemd actually has tonnes of interesting features, that I think are even more useful for running throwaway agent-written code.
Note this is all Linux only - sorry Mac users, there's no real equivalent of systemd on macOS (launchd covers some of the cron-style stuff, but not the resource limits).
Easy memory/CPU caps per process

You may have experienced this before. You have an agent write a script, perhaps to do some data analysis. It has a terrible memory leak, and suddenly your machine freezes and (hopefully) the kernel resumes after a bit with an OOM error.

I've had this a few times, and it's very annoying. Turns out systemd has an easy way to limit processes and any subprocesses, with MemoryMax and CPUQuota.   These actually use the same underlying cgroup limits as Docker would.
If you want to for example run Claude Code with 4GB of memory max and only 2 CPU cores to avoid it burning through all your RAM, it's as simple as running this:
systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=4G -p CPUQuota=200% claude
You can obviously run any command this way. Bonus point, if you use systemd-cgtop instead of top (or btop), you can see memory use and CPU use per cgroup.

PS: systemd does also have sandboxing features (ProtectHome, ReadWritePaths and friends), which you'd think would be perfect for agents. But there are so many footguns with it that it's too long to explain in this article - I'll maybe do a follow up one day.
Limiting how long a process can run for

Similarly to the above, if you want to limit e.g. an autonomous agent to only run for 30min max, you can just use the RuntimeMaxSec argument. For example, if you want to run OpenCode to investigate something but don't want it spending more than 30 minutes, you can simply run:

systemd-run --user --same-dir --unit=opencode-agent \
  -p RuntimeMaxSec=30m \
  ~/.opencode/bin/opencode run --standalone --auto \
  "Fix the failing tests in this repo and summarise what you changed"

# follow it:   journalctl --user -u opencode-agent -f
NB: the --standalone arg is required, because OpenCode by default will run its work on a background server which you may already have running, which will bypass the time limit.
Inhibiting sleep

This one is likely more useful for laptops, but if you want to run a process and close your laptop, systemd-inhibit is a good way to do that. You can combine with the former one to make sure it expires after a while to avoid draining your battery entirely:

systemd-run --user --same-dir --unit=claude-agent \
  -p RuntimeMaxSec=30m \
  systemd-inhibit --what=sleep:idle:handle-lid-switch --why="claude agent run" \
  ~/.local/bin/claude -p \
  "Fix the failing tests in this repo and summarise what you changed"
Better cron

More obvious, but systemd has a lot of features that a simple cron doesn't. I'd recommend reading the full man page for full details, but there are some cool features there. For example, one I use all the time is Persistent, so if your computer is off/sleeping, it will run the task when it comes back online. This is really useful if like me you want an agent to summarise something and notify you every week.

Equally, the OnSuccess and OnFailure arguments are helpful. If you define a slack or email unit, you can easily pipe results of runs. It's also a good place to put 'dead man's handle' calls to the likes of Healthchecks.io.

Another nice one is adding a random delay to your cron jobs, if you have a bunch of machines hitting a service at say 1am. You can have it randomly delay the start a bit with RandomizedDelaySec to avoid a huge spike in load.
Path units
This is a really cool one I did not know about until I researched this article. Effectively it fires when something in a folder changes.

# ~/.config/systemd/user/agent-inbox.path
[Path]
DirectoryNotEmpty=%h/agent-inbox

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target

# ~/.config/systemd/user/agent-inbox.service
[Unit]
OnSuccess=slack-notify.service

[Service]
Type=exec
RuntimeMaxSec=30m
MemoryMax=4G
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c YOUR_COMMAND_HERE

So you could use this for watching a folder, and every time it changes, triggering something. If you have a folder of e.g. expenses or invoices, you can just drop files in there and have the agent categorise them for you as new files get added.

Overall, if like me you thought systemd was only really useful for running daemons and not much more, it's definitely worth diving into. Often it provides a lot of the plumbing you need without having to roll your own, especially for the huge amount of almost "disposable" software you tend to end up with these days.
